_comment: The benzodiazepine discontinuation reference's population timing bands, and the clinical acting-class floor for the drugs a reader is most likely to have logged. One file because the two tables are one fact split in half: `actingClasses` says which band a named drug belongs to, `bands` says what that band's half-life interval and onset/peak windows are, and a class naming a band the other file does not define is a broken screen.
citation: Navarrete F, Garcia-Gutierrez MS, Gasparyan A, Manzanares J. Benzodiazepine Dependence: Clinical and Molecular Aspects, Preventive Strategies and Therapeutic Approaches. Int J Mol Sci. 2026;27(3):1430; doi:10.3390/ijms27031430
_units: Half-life boundaries are minutes (the unit every half-life in this database carries). Onset and peak windows are hours, one unit for all three bands so the boundaries stay comparable; the reader-facing phrase picks days or hours for itself and is localized copy keyed by the band.
_uncited_rule: A band's timing window ships only with a citation that states it. `citation: false` means the window is absent, not that a number is being shown uncited — the columns are nullable and the screen renders nothing for a band with no window.

bands.notes: Peak at 4-7 days, measured — the long-half-life arm of the same Rickels 1990 trial (pmid:2222129): 'peak severity at 2 days for short half-life and 4 to 7 days for long half-life benzodiazepines.' This replaces a 5-14 day window that overshot it and cited nothing. Onset is absent because nothing survives checking: NAV26 Sec. 5.4 gives 2-3 days (short) and 5-10 days (long), which are at or past Rickels' MEASURED peak for the same classes — onset cannot follow peak, so at least one of the two is mislabelled, and the 2026 narrative review loses to the 1990 double-blind trial with daily assessments. The 6-24 h short onset this replaced was clinically plausible and sourced to nothing at all. The 40 h boundary approximates NAV26 Table 2's Long Acting group, but the review states no threshold and its groups are not threshold-separable.

No timing window: Rickels 1990 measured two half-life arms, short and long, and there is no intermediate one to take a peak from. NAV26 Sec. 5.4 gives no intermediate band either. The band still exists to classify a drug, because the half-life boundaries place one; it just has nothing to say about when withdrawal peaks, and says nothing rather than interpolating between the two arms.

Peak at 2 days, measured. Rickels 1990 (pmid:2222129, `papers` closed — the abstract states the figure) abruptly discontinued 57 benzodiazepine-dependent patients on >1 year of daily use, double-blind against continued dosing, assessing daily: 'peak severity at 2 days for short half-life and 4 to 7 days for long half-life benzodiazepines.' Onset is absent because nothing survives checking: NAV26 Sec. 5.4 gives 2-3 days (short) and 5-10 days (long), which are at or past Rickels' MEASURED peak for the same classes — onset cannot follow peak, so at least one of the two is mislabelled, and the 2026 narrative review loses to the 1990 double-blind trial with daily assessments. The 6-24 h short onset this replaced was clinically plausible and sourced to nothing at all. The 12 h boundary approximates NAV26 Table 2's Short Acting group but overlaps its Intermediate group, so no threshold reproduces the review's own classification; the boundary is Piru's, not the review's.

actingClasses.notes: NAV26 Table 2, Long Acting: t-half 40-200 h, active metabolites.

NAV26 Table 2, Long Acting: t-half 40-100 h, active metabolites. Its own parent half-life in this database is 600 min (10 h), which the half-life boundaries alone would read as short — the clinical floor is what carries it, and the nordazepam tail is why.
NAV26 Table 2, Long Acting: t-half 18-50 h.

Absent from NAV26 Table 2 entirely, so the review does not place it in any band, and no other primary source classifies temazepam into a named acting-class band either. The FDA label gives a biphasic decline with terminal half-life 3.5-18.4 h (mean 8.8 h; DailyMed setid 066e25b2-8a1b-4b08-b585-ce36753bf104) and Ashton Table 1 gives 8-22 h -- both wide enough to bracket this database's own 900 min (15 h) without confirming it, and the label's mean sits below it. So 15 h is non-contradicted rather than corroborated. It falls inside the intermediate boundary under every source's range, and intermediate carries no timing window, so nothing is shown that a reader could be misled by. Still the citation that is missing, not the number.

NAV26 Table 2, Short Acting: t-half 6-10 h. Moved from intermediate 2026-08-28 after three independent sources agreed and none dissented: the review's own table, the FDA label ('The mean elimination half-life for oxazepam was approximately 8.2 hours (range 5.7 to 10.9 hours)', DailyMed setid 03440821-831c-4085-98f9-faa88e98c503), and this database's own 480 min (8 h). Ashton Table 1 gives 4-15 h, consistent, though Ashton has no acting-class column at all -- it carries raw half-life ranges and an unrelated market-aim axis, so it offers no second opinion on the taxonomy. Note what the move does beyond the label: `short` carries a peak-timing window, so oxazepam now shows 'peaks around 2 days'. Rickels 1990's abstract does not name which benzodiazepines were in its short arm, so that attachment is a class-level inference -- the same one already made for every other member of this band, not a new kind of claim.
NAV26 Table 2, Intermediate Acting: t-half 11-22 h.
NAV26 Table 2, Ultra-Short Acting: t-half 1.5-5.5 h. Folded into short because these bands carry no ultra-short.
NAV26 Table 2, Short Acting: t-half 12-15 h.

NAV26 Table 2, Short Acting: t-half 10-20 h. This database's half-life (840 min = 14 h) crosses the 12 h boundary, so the boundaries alone would read it as intermediate — the clinical floor is why it stays short, and the review agrees with the floor.
